summary:
EASV Space Health AI explores how astronauts on long-duration missions could access and understand health information when immediate medical support from Earth is limited.

Our proposed approach combines an individual health profile, physiological indicators, accessible visualization, and local artificial intelligence to support health awareness and greater autonomy. Future development would integrate compatible sensors, medically reviewed reference materials, and persistent records.

The working MVP demonstrates this concept through a fictional astronaut, Alex Morgan, and simulated health measurements. A local AI assistant answers questions in English and Spanish, retrieves selected passages from NASA reports on sleep, circadian rhythms, and ionizing radiation, and provides source references. Text and voice interaction make the information accessible through a web dashboard.

The AI runs locally; the profile and measurements are simulated. Wearable acquisition, longitudinal monitoring, and record synchronization remain proposed extensions rather than completed features.

Inspired by NASA’s Human Research Program, the project investigates a human-centered approach to astronaut health information. It does not replace medical professionals, provide clinical diagnoses, or prescribe treatment. Operational use would require further technical, medical, security, and accessibility validation.
details:
EASV Space Health AI

Project overview

EASV Space Health AI is an experimental astronaut health-monitoring and information-support concept with a functioning local-AI MVP.

We are participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge **Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions**. Our proposed contribution is to bring individual health information, accessible visualization, and relevant scientific knowledge into one astronaut-centered environment, supporting greater awareness and autonomy when immediate assistance from Earth is limited.

Our guiding principle is:

In deep space, communication can fail. Access to health information should continue.

The broader vision includes compatible physiological sensors, individual records, and medically reviewed reference material. The current demonstration explores part of that vision through a simulated health profile, a visual dashboard, bilingual interaction, and an AI assistant running on our own computing hardware.

The problem we address

Long-duration missions place astronauts farther from immediate terrestrial support. Health information can come from different devices, personal observations, and reference materials, making it difficult to review it as a coherent individual picture.

NASA's Human Research Program describes five major hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity changes, and hostile or closed environments. These hazards provide the conceptual context for our proposal.

We want to investigate how local computing and AI could help an astronaut access relevant information, understand available measurements, and recognize missing information without depending continuously on an external cloud AI service.

How we propose to address it

The proposed platform would organize information around an individual astronaut profile and combine:

- Measurements from compatible and appropriately validated physiological devices.

- Personal records and manually entered observations.

- A clear visual presentation of available information and, in future versions, recorded changes over time.

- A local AI assistant that relates supplied information to relevant reference material.

- Text and voice interaction to make information easier to access.

- Future mechanisms for local record persistence and controlled synchronization.

Potential measurements include heart rate, oxygen saturation, sleep duration, physical activity, blood pressure, and glucose, depending on the measurement device and its validated capabilities. We do not assume that a smartwatch can measure all these indicators.

The intended contribution is the integration of these elements into a coherent, accessible environment. We are not claiming to have invented a medical sensor or a diagnostic method.

What the current MVP demonstrates

The MVP is a local web application backed by a Python service and GPT-OSS 20B, running through LM Studio on our development workstation.

The demonstration uses Alex Morgan, a fictional profile. All displayed health values are simulated. Oxygen saturation and muscle and bone assessments are explicitly marked as unavailable rather than filled with invented measurements.

The working prototype includes:

- An anatomical-style dashboard with an illustrative astronaut and animated visual indicators.

- A fixed simulated profile that the assistant can summarize.

- Questions and answers in Spanish and English, following the language of the current question.

- Retrieval of selected passages from locally stored NASA reports, with references that open the corresponding source page.

- Local speech recognition and speech synthesis.

- A voice workflow that ends recording after approximately 2.5 seconds of silence following detected speech, transcribes the question, sends it to the assistant, and attempts to play the response automatically.

- Access from the workstation and devices on the same private local network.

The anatomical illustration, moving trace, and other animations are presentation elements. They are not live physiological signals, measured ECG recordings, or clinical assessments. The current application does not collect wearable measurements, edit patient records, or calculate health trends.

The local language model and its generated responses are real. The fictional elements are the profile and its health measurements. The model receives the selected reference passages and simulated profile as context during each question; it has not been trained or fine-tuned on these documents.

Scientific resources and knowledge retrieval

The following NASA pages inform the problem definition and conceptual requirements:

- [Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight](https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/hazards/)

- [Risks of Human Spaceflight](https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/risks/)

- [Ongoing Human Research Program Research](https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/ongoing-hrp-research/)

The implemented documentary pilot uses selected passages from two NASA Human Research Program reports:

1. Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload** — public release dated April 11, 2016. The pilot retrieves passages from PDF page 4, the executive summary. This is historical evidence, not a claim to provide the latest clinical guidance. [Official report](https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/Evidence/reports/Sleep.pdf)

2. Risk of Ionizing Radiation Carcinogenesis** — public release identified as 2026. The pilot retrieves passages from PDF page 10, the executive summary. [Official report](https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/evidence/reports/HRP-ER-CANCER-SR-20260811.pdf)

The current searchable corpus contains five fragments from those two reviewed pages. Although the original PDF files are stored locally, their entire contents are not enabled for retrieval. The three general NASA web pages above are conceptual references, not live search sources for the assistant.

The assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG: it reformulates search terms, retrieves passages through a local lexical index, and generates an answer using the supplied context. Reference identifiers are checked against the retrieved passages. This structural check does not independently establish medical correctness or guarantee that every generated statement is supported.

The reference collection could later be expanded with material selected and reviewed by a qualified medical team. NASA sources do not validate the simulated values on the dashboard, endorse the project, or establish an official partnership.

Local processing and voice access

The current runtime uses local components for language-model inference, document retrieval, speech recognition, and speech synthesis. Development tools and initial downloads used Internet connectivity. We have not completed a full disconnected cold-start acceptance test, so we distinguish local processing from a fully validated offline deployment.

On the workstation, the application is accessible through a loopback browser address. Private-network access allows phones and tablets to use the workstation as the processing server; the language model does not run independently on those devices.

Microphone access over the local network requires a trusted HTTPS connection and explicit device permission. A local HTTPS setup is prepared for mobile testing. Audio playback may also require a user gesture under browser policies. Written responses and playback controls remain available.

Speech recognition uses multilingual Whisper base through faster-whisper on the workstation CPU. Speech synthesis uses installed Windows voices in the response language. Incoming recordings are processed in memory rather than saved as user audio files. Transcription errors remain possible, especially with noise, names, numbers, and units.

Boundaries and human oversight

This is a simulation-based research and demonstration prototype. It is not a clinically validated medical decision-support system, does not replace a physician, and is not intended for autonomous diagnosis, treatment prescription, or determining fitness for duty.

The assistant is instructed to acknowledge insufficient evidence and avoid inventing missing measurements or citations. Limited tests have exercised these behaviors; they do not guarantee the absence of errors.

Any future safety-critical alerts would require validated rules, medical oversight, and established mission procedures. Such alerts must not depend solely on unrestricted generative output. No validated clinical alert system is implemented in this MVP.

The prototype is used with fictitious data. It does not yet implement production patient authentication, role-based access, longitudinal medical-record management, or a complete health-data security framework. Private-network restrictions and optional HTTPS are development protections, not a claim of clinical or aerospace certification.

Proposed architecture beyond the demonstration

The future design separates device acquisition, individual records, visualization, local AI, synchronization, and security so that each can be developed and evaluated independently.

Device acquisition: integrate selected compatible sensors and preserve measurement units, timestamps, device identity, and quality indicators.

Individual records: associate measurements and observations with the correct person, retaining provenance and distinguishing missing information from measured values.

Visualization: provide usable views of measurements and actual recorded trends, with accessibility review.

Local AI: expand the reviewed reference collection and evaluate context-aware explanations under medical and operational oversight.

Persistence and synchronization: investigate reliable local storage and later transfer to authorized systems, including record identifiers, duplicate prevention, integrity checks, and conflict handling.

Security: implement and test authentication, access control, encryption, consent, retention policies, and protection of real health information before such data is introduced.

These are proposed extensions. They are not presented as completed sensor, record-management, or synchronization capabilities.

Development environment and validation

The current development workstation uses Windows 11 Professional, a Ryzen 5 5600X processor, 32 GB DDR4 RAM, an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB VRAM, and an RTX 2060 Super with 8 GB VRAM. The reported LM Studio version is 0.4.28 build 2. Both GPUs were observed participating in the local model runs; that observation does not establish that using both is faster than using one.

The application uses Python, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a SQLite FTS5 document index. The current AI candidate is GPT-OSS 20B MXFP4. Alternative models were evaluated before selecting this candidate.

Completed development checks include small bilingual model-evaluation sets, a ten-case documentary pilot, panel integration checks, source-file integrity checks, and browser inspection. Voice generation, recognition, and the automatic interaction flow were tested using synthetic local audio. A silence-only test confirmed that no question was submitted without detected speech.

The project owner also confirmed using the AI from a phone on the same Wi-Fi network and reported a satisfactory response experience. This is distinct from formal microphone validation on every target device.

Physical voice testing across PC, Android phone, iPhone, and Android tablet remains to be recorded systematically. Other work includes independent medical review, broader retrieval evaluation, accessibility testing with target users, reliability testing, and security assessment.

Development roadmap

Current stage: a working local web MVP with a simulated profile, animated dashboard, documentary AI interaction, and local voice components.

Next stage: validate the demonstration workflow on the target devices and address observed usability, transcription, and source-support issues without expanding beyond the MVP's purpose.

Later stages: expand medically reviewed content, integrate selected physiological devices, implement persistent individual records, and test synchronization and operational resilience.

Before real-world use: complete appropriate medical, technical, security, accessibility, and aerospace evaluation. A future Android application or independent phone-based inference would require additional development; the current mobile interface is browser-based and relies on the workstation.

Disclosure of artificial intelligence use

ChatGPT and Codex from OpenAI assisted with architecture proposals, documentation, software implementation, investigation of official references, test preparation and execution, and iterative corrections. The team defined the problem and scope, supplied visual direction, evaluated the experience, and requested changes.

The runtime uses GPT-OSS 20B for language processing and answer generation, Whisper base for local speech recognition, and installed Windows speech voices for audio output. The astronaut illustration was generated with an OpenAI image-generation tool. The interface icons and animations were implemented in web code with AI assistance.

AI-assisted development and generated illustrations are distinct from the local AI demonstrated in the application. No clinical or diagnostic training was performed by the team. Additional tools used to prepare presentation material should be declared in the relevant submission fields.

Our intended contribution

We believe future exploration will require resilient and human-centered ways to access health information. EASV Space Health AI explores one contribution: bringing an astronaut's available information and relevant scientific references closer together through local, accessible interaction.

The MVP is an initial demonstration of this direction. Its potential depends on further development and responsible validation with medical and domain specialists.

Exploring the universe means caring for the people who make exploration possible.
